reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: A urethral stricture is a fibrotic narrowing of the urethral lumen, largely a condition of the male anterior urethra, presenting with obstructive voiding symptoms such as a weak, splayed, or spraying stream, straining, and incomplete emptying

Common causes include prior instrumentation or catheterisation, straddle and pelvic trauma, infection (historically gonococcal urethritis), and lichen sclerosus affecting the meatus and distal urethra
Symptoms overlap with prostatic obstruction, but a young man or a history of trauma, catheterisation, or urethritis should raise suspicion of stricture
Uroflowmetry classically shows a prolonged, low, plateau-shaped flow curve, and retrograde urethrography with voiding studies defines the site, length, and number of strictures
Complications include recurrent urinary infection, bladder stones, diverticula, and, in longstanding severe disease, back-pressure effects on the upper tracts and acute retention

Management principles depend on stricture length and location: dilatation or internal urethrotomy for short strictures, and urethroplasty for longer, recurrent, or complex disease, which offers the most durable cure
Repeated dilatation or urethrotomy for recurrent strictures tends to fail and may worsen fibrosis, so early referral for reconstructive urethroplasty is preferred in appropriate cases
Meatal or distal strictures should prompt evaluation for lichen sclerosus
reference.pathophysiology: A urethral stricture is the result of scarring within the corpus spongiosum (spongiofibrosis) and urethral epithelium following injury or inflammation. Trauma, infection, instrumentation, or inflammatory disease such as lichen sclerosus provokes healing by fibrosis, which contracts and narrows the lumen. The narrowed segment increases outflow resistance, causing high-pressure voiding, turbulent flow, and incomplete emptying. Persistent obstruction leads to proximal urethral dilatation, bladder wall changes, stasis with infection and stone formation, and in severe cases upper tract dilatation and retention.
additionalDifferentials: Benign prostatic hyperplasia / bladder outlet obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Uroflowmetry demonstrating a low, plateau-shaped flow pattern
Retrograde urethrography with voiding cystourethrography to localise and measure the stricture
Flexible urethroscopy to inspect the stricture directly
Urinalysis and culture for associated infection
Post-void residual and renal tract ultrasound to assess retention and upper tracts
Assessment for lichen sclerosus in distal or meatal strictures
redFlags: Acute urinary retention from a tight stricture, a urological emergency requiring urgent drainage
Obstructive uropathy with upper tract dilatation and renal impairment
Recurrent urinary infection, periurethral abscess, or urethral fistula
Failure of a difficult catheterisation, which should prompt suprapubic drainage rather than forceful attempts
Suspicion of urethral malignancy in an atypical or non-healing stricture
reference.prognosis: Short strictures may respond to dilatation or urethrotomy but recurrence is common; urethroplasty provides high long-term success for suitable strictures, whereas complex, recurrent, or lichen sclerosus-associated disease can require staged or repeated reconstruction.
pitfalls: Attributing obstructive symptoms to the prostate in a younger man and missing a stricture
Repeated dilatation or urethrotomy for recurrent strictures, worsening scarring and delaying definitive repair
Forcing a urethral catheter through a stricture, risking false passage and injury
Overlooking lichen sclerosus in distal strictures
Failing to assess the upper tracts and renal function in longstanding obstruction
